passages.happening:
The Teacher tests pleasure. ‘But it proved to be futile’ (verse 1). Of laughter he says it is folly, and of pleasure, what does it achieve (verse 2). He cheers himself with wine while keeping his mind on wisdom, to see what is worth doing ‘during the few days of their lives’ (verse 3).

Then he builds. ‘I built houses and planted vineyards for myself’ (verse 4). ‘I made gardens and parks for myself, where I planted all kinds of fruit trees’ (verse 5). He builds reservoirs, gains servants, herds and flocks, silver and gold and the treasure of kings, singers, and many concubines (verses 6-8). ‘So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me’ (verse 9). ‘Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself’ (verse 10).

Then he looks at it all. ‘Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 announced the search. Chapter 2 carries it out. Speaking as a king with unlimited means, the Teacher tries every path people take to find satisfaction: pleasure, achievement, wealth, wisdom. Whether or not Solomon wrote these words, the chapter uses a royal voice to test life at its most privileged. If even the richest and wisest king in Israel's memory found no lasting gain, no one else will.

Royal parks were symbols of power in the ancient world. Assyrian and Persian kings planted vast parks stocked with trees and animals from across their empires, watered by canals and reservoirs. In a land with little rain, reservoirs were major feats of engineering. A large household of wives and concubines was a sign of royal status, and a way to seal alliances through marriage.

The word for parks in verse 5, pardes, is a loanword from Persian, and the same word eventually gave English the word paradise. Notice how often he says he did it for himself. The experiment is centered on the self from start to finish.
passages.later: The Bible remembers Solomon's wealth in the same terms: ‘King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom’ (1 Kings 10:23). And John warns about the desire behind verse 10: ‘The world is passing away, along with its desires’ (1 John 2:17).
passages.asks: The Teacher had everything and found no gain. Ask what you are sure would satisfy you if only you had it. And ask what it would mean to hold even good things knowing they cannot be your final gain.

passages.t: One fate for the wise and the fool
passages.happening:
The Teacher weighs wisdom against folly. ‘And I saw that wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness’ (verse 13). ‘The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both’ (verse 14).

Both are forgotten, and “the wise man will die just like the fool!” (verse 16). Then comes his rawest cry: ‘So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me’ (verse 17).

He hates what he has worked for, because he must leave it to someone who comes after him, ‘And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish?’ (verse 19). ‘So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun’ (verse 20). ‘Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Wisdom is better than folly. The Teacher never denies it. But death comes to both, and both are forgotten. Fate here is miqreh, what happens to a person, and above all, death.

Inheritance mattered greatly in the ancient world. Property passed to sons, and a man's legacy was tied to what he left. Solomon's own son, Rehoboam, lost most of his father's kingdom through foolish choices (1 Kings 12), a story that gives verse 19 a sharp edge for anyone who knew it.

Verse 17 is the darkest cry in the chapter. The Bible records it honestly, as the cry of a man whose work could not carry the weight he had put on it. It is not counsel. And it is not the chapter's last word.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Verse 23 describes something many people know: days full of grief, and a mind that will not rest even at night.
passages.later: The psalm describes the same restless labor: ‘In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat’ (Psalm 127:2), and the psalm adds that God gives sleep to those he loves. And Elijah, under the broom tree, also asked to die, and God answered him with bread and sleep (1 Kings 19:4-8).
passages.asks: The Teacher's mind would not rest at night. Ask what keeps your mind awake, and whether you have told anyone. And ask what you are building that you will one day have to leave to someone else, and how you might hold it more lightly.

passages.happening:
Then the chapter turns. “Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God” (verse 24). ‘For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?’ (verse 25).

To the person who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy. To the sinner he gives the task of gathering and storing up, only to hand it over to someone who pleases God. ‘This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
For the first time a new note sounds, one that will return throughout the book. The ordinary goods of food, drink and work are gifts from God, and apart from him no one can enjoy them. The chapter moves from grasping at everything to receiving something.

Joy here is simchah. It was tested and found wanting as a final gain at the start of the chapter. At the end it comes back as a gift.

The last verse still ends with ‘futile’. Even this answer does not settle every question. The book will keep asking.
passages.later: The book returns to this note again and again, and most clearly in chapter 8: there is ‘nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry’ (Ecclesiastes 8:15). And Paul tells the rich to hope in ‘God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy’ (1 Timothy 6:17).
passages.hard:
Is the Teacher recommending that people eat, drink and be merry because life is pointless?

Verse 24 says nothing is better than to eat, drink and enjoy one's work. Out of context, this could sound like resigned pleasure-seeking: since nothing lasts, enjoy what you can. Some interpreters read the book's enjoyment passages that way, as a sad second-best in a futile world.

But the verse goes on to say that this is from the hand of God, and verse 25 adds that apart from him no one can find enjoyment. Many interpreters therefore read these passages as the book's positive counsel: receive ordinary goods as God's gifts, instead of trying to squeeze ultimate meaning out of them. The difference from mere pleasure-seeking is that the joy is received from God, not grabbed as a substitute for him.

The chapter's last verse still ends with futility, so even this answer does not resolve every question. It is a place to stand, not the end of the search.
passages.asks: Food, drink and work are from the hand of God. Ask whether you received today's ordinary gifts as gifts, or only noticed what was missing. And ask whom you could share a simple meal with this week, with thanks.
